extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for USPTO examiners on identifying, analyzing, and making statutory and nonstatutory (obviousness-type) double patenting rejections, including when to use provisional rejections, terminal disclaimers, and specific form paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory double patenting (same invention) — use of provisional rejection (¶ 8.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] provisionally rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as claiming the same invention as that of claim [2] of copending Application No. [3] (reference application). This is a provisional statutory double patenting rejection since the claims directed to the same invention have not in fact been patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 8.30 and is used only for double patenting rejections of the same invention claimed in another copending application (scope of claimed inventions identical). Do not use this paragraph where the claims directed to the same invention are in an issued patent (use form paragraph 8.31 instead). May be used where the patent and application under examination: (a) name the same inventive entity, (b) name different inventive entities but are commonly assigned, (c) are not commonly assigned but name at least one common inventor, (d) are filed by a common applicant, (e) claim patentably indistinct inventions made under a joint research agreement (pre-AIA 103(c)), or (f) claim patentably indistinct inventions with common ownership timing requirements under AIA. For pre-AIA and AIA prosecutions, additional specific form paragraphs (e.g., 8.27.fti, 8.27.aia, 7.15.02.fti) may be required as noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting (NSDP) — definition and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on nonstatutory double patenting is a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy to prevent unjustified or improper timewise extension of the right to exclude granted by a patent. NSDP is appropriate where conflicting claims are not identical but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined claim is anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding whether NSDP is appropriate, first ask whether any invention claimed in the application is anticipated by or is an obvious variation of an invention claimed in the patent. The examiner should construe the claims in the application and the reference to determine differences and then determine patentable distinctness using anticipation and/or obviousness analyses (see Pfizer v. Teva and cited cases). A timely filed terminal disclaimer may overcome an NSDP rejection if requirements are met (see separate rubric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of reference patent/application disclosure in NSDP analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: No part of the reference patent or application may be used as if it were prior art when considering whether an application claim would have been anticipated by or is an obvious variation of the invention in a reference. This does not preclude all use of the reference disclosure to understand the meaning of the reference claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification may be used as a dictionary to learn the meaning of a term (Toro Co.; Renishaw; Phillips). Portions of the specification that provide support for the reference claims may be examined and considered when addressing whether a claim in the application defines an obvious variation of an invention claimed in the reference (In re Vogel). However, subject matter disclosed in the reference that does not fall within the scope of a reference claim cannot be used to support an NSDP rejection (that would treat the reference as prior art). When construing reference claims, determine which portions of the disclosure fall within the claim scope and limit consideration to those portions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation analysis for NSDP
rubrics_metrics.description: NSDP is appropriate where a claim in an application claims subject matter that is different but not patentably distinct from subject matter claimed in a prior patent or copending application because the claim under examination is anticipated by the reference claim(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This arises when, for example, the examined claim is generic to a species or sub-genus claimed in the conflicting patent/application (entire scope of the reference claim falls within scope of examined claim). In such cases an obviousness analysis is not required; the NSDP rejection should explain that the species or sub-genus in the conflicting patent or application anticipates the claimed genus and that issuing the genus would improperly extend the right to exclude. In genus-species or overlapping-scope situations where anticipation cannot be established, an obviousness analysis is typically required and the examiner should explain why it would have been obvious to select the claimed species given the genus (see MPEP § 2131.02 and § 2144.08).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness analysis for NSDP (Graham factors and content of rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where NSDP is not based on anticipation or an unjustified timewise extension rationale, it is analogous to the nonobviousness inquiry of 35 U.S.C. 103 except the patent disclosure is not prior art. The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere should be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider: (A) scope and content of the patent claim relative to the application claim; (B) differences between the claims; (C) level of ordinary skill in the art; (D) objective indicia of nonobviousness. Any NSDP rejection under an obviousness analysis should clearly state (A) the differences between the inventions defined by the conflicting claims and (B) the reasons why a person of ordinary skill would conclude the claimed invention is an obvious variation. Any secondary references used to support the obviousness analysis must be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 (see MPEP §§ 2120, 2141).

rubrics_metrics.name: One-way test for distinctness (when only one directional determination is needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent term filing date of the application under examination is the same or later than that of a reference application or patent, only a one-way determination of distinctness is needed — i.e., whether the invention claimed in the application would have been anticipated by or an obvious variation of the invention claimed in the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a one-way test in these circumstances (see In re Berg). Even if the application under examination has the earlier patent term filing date, a one-way determination suffices absent a finding that (A) the PTO is solely responsible for any delays in prosecution (In re Hubbell) and (B) the applicant could not have filed the conflicting claims in a single earlier-filed application (In re Kaplan). If one-way test supports that the application claim would have been obvious over the patent claim, NSDP rejection is proper to prevent unjustified timewise extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer as remedy to overcome NSDP
rubrics_metrics.description: A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) or 1.321(d) may be used to overcome an actual or provisional rejection based on NSDP provided the reference application or patent is commonly owned with the examined application or claims an invention made as a result of activities under a joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimer must be signed in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(b). Filing a terminal disclaimer alone is not a complete reply; it must be accompanied by a reply requesting reconsideration of the prior Office action. For replies to non-final Office actions follow 37 CFR 1.111(a); for replies to final Office actions follow 37 CFR 1.113(c). See MPEP § 1490 for guidance regarding terminal disclaimers and withdrawal of NSDP rejections when these are the only rejections remaining. USPTO provides terminal disclaimer forms and eTerminal Disclaimer processing information on the website (forms PTO/SB/25, PTO/SB/26, PTO/AIA/25, PTO/AIA/26 depending on filing date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph and procedural use requirements for NSDP rejections (¶ 8.33 - 8.39)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 8.33 ('Basis for Nonstatutory Double Patenting, Heading Only') must precede any of form paragraphs 8.34 to 8.39 and be used only once in an Office action. Specific form paragraphs (8.34–8.39) are used to make particular NSDP rejections depending on whether the reference is a patent or a copending application and whether secondary references are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 8.34 for NSDP rejections based on a patent (no secondary reference), 8.35 for provisional NSDP rejections based on a copending application (no secondary reference), and other form paragraphs (8.36–8.39) where secondary references or equitable principles apply. Use appropriate additional form paragraphs for pre-AIA (fti) or AIA (aia) circumstances (e.g., 8.27.fti, 8.28.fti, 7.21.fti, 7.15.02.fti) as noted in examiner notes. Provide required bracketed insertions (claim numbers, patent/application numbers, explanation for anticipation or obviousness rationale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable/principles-based NSDP (unjustified timewise extension) and special approvals (Schneller/Schneller-type)
rubrics_metrics.description: NSDP may also be based on equitable principles to prevent unjustified timewise extension of the patent term when issuance of a second patent would provide such an unjustified extension (e.g., claims to methods of use versus claims to compounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Geneva Pharmaceuticals and Schneller illustrate situations where disclosure outside the claim scope might nevertheless justify an equitable NSDP rejection. Schneller-type rejections will be rare and require consultation with the supervisory patent examiner (SPE) and approval of the Technology Center (TC) Director before making such a rejection. Each equitable NSDP situation must be decided on its own facts and the examiner should refer to subsection II.B.6 for detailed discussion.
